requirement_title: Generator and analyzer crash with IndexOutOfRangeException on a closed generic struct from a referenced assembly
requirement_text:
# REQ-2283: Generator and analyzer crash with IndexOutOfRangeException on a closed generic struct from a referenced assembly

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2283
Type: bug

## Requirement

Both `MessagePackGenerator` (CS8785) and `MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer` (AD0001) throw `IndexOutOfRangeException` when a `[MessagePackObject]` type has a member whose type is a closed generic value type defined in a referenced assembly.

Because the generator then "will not contribute to the output", the compiling assembly silently ends up with no generated resolver at all. It is only a warning, so a normal build looks fine, but trimmed and NativeAOT apps fail at runtime.

Repro: two projects. `lib`:

```csharp
using MessagePack;
namespace Lib;

[MessagePackObject]
public partial record struct Item<T>([property: Key(0)] string Key);
```

`app`, with a `ProjectReference` to `lib`:

```csharp
using MessagePack; using Lib;
namespace App;

[MessagePackObject]
public sealed partial record Cmd([property: Key(0)] string Scope)
{
    [Key(1)] public Item<int> Member { get; init; }
}
```

Then `dotnet build` on `app`.

Expected: a clean build, with a generated resolver in `app`.

Actual:

```
CSC : warning CS8785: Generator 'MessagePackGenerator' failed to generate source. It will not
contribute to the output and compilation errors may occur as a result. Exception was of type
'IndexOutOfRangeException' with message 'Index was outside the bounds of the array.'.
CSC : warning AD0001: Analyzer 'MessagePack.SourceGenerator.Analyzers.MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer'
threw an exception of type 'System.IndexOutOfRangeException' with message 'Index was outside the
bounds of the array.'.
```

`app.dll` contains no `GeneratedMessagePackResolver`. Version used: MessagePack 3.1.8.

What triggers it (`Item` declared in `lib`, `Cmd` in `app`):

| `Item` declared as | result |
|---|---|
| `record struct Item<T>` | crash |
| `struct Item<T>` | crash |
| `struct Item` | ok |
| `record struct Item` | ok |
| `class Item<T>` | ok |
| `record class Item<T>` | ok |

It needs all three of: generic, value type, from a referenced assembly. Moving the identical `Item<T>` declaration into `app` makes the crash disappear.

Reporter's analysis: `CollectGeneric` line 661 is the closed-generic branch that calls `GetObjectInfo` directly, so `GetObjectInfo` runs against a type that has no syntax. Several diagnostic paths inside it index `DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0]` directly (lines 735, 1009, 1101) instead of using `FirstOrDefault()` like the neighbouring `GetIdentifierLocation` / `GetLocation` / `GetParameterListLocation` helpers. That collection is empty for a metadata symbol. The reporter did not narrow down which of the three fires.

Workaround: `[MessagePackFormatter(typeof(ItemFormatter<>))]` on the generic value type short-circuits `CollectCore` before `GetObjectInfo` is reached.

## Acceptance criteria

- Building `app` from the repro produces no CS8785 warning. (derived)
- Building `app` from the repro produces no AD0001 warning from `MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer`. (derived)
- `app.dll` contains a `GeneratedMessagePackResolver` (a generated resolver exists). (derived)
- The generator and analyzer do not throw on a closed generic struct or record struct declared in a referenced assembly.
- Closed generic classes, non-generic structs and types declared in the same assembly keep working as before (the "ok" rows in the table). (derived)
- Diagnostics that need a source location do not crash when the offending symbol has no declaring syntax (metadata symbol). (derived)

## Notes from discussion

No comments on the issue. The reporter points at `DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0]` being indexed unguarded at TypeCollector.cs lines 735, 1009 and 1101, and notes the neighbouring helpers use `FirstOrDefault()`. Possibly related: #2092 (CS8785 from the v3 generator, different inner exception, no repro).

findings.claim: The new early return in CollectGeneric uses `type.OriginalDefinition.DeclaringSyntaxReferences.IsEmpty` to decide that a generic type comes from a referenced assembly. That only holds for PE/metadata references. When `Lib` is referenced as a CompilationReference, which is how project-to-project references appear in the IDE, `Item<T>` still has syntax references. The guard then does not fire, and the closed-generic path runs `GetObjectInfo` on a type from another compilation. The result is that the IDE and the command-line build collect and generate different things for the same project (and possibly an AD0001 in the IDE). The check should compare `type.ContainingAssembly` with `compilation.Assembly`.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.MetadataVsCompilationReferenceGenericStructTests.GeneratedOutputIsSameForImageAndCompilationReference. It compiles Lib once and runs MessagePackGenerator over App with Lib as an emitted image reference and then as a CompilationReference. It asserts there is no generator exception and that the generated sources are identical.

findings.claim: The early-return guard for generic types without declaring syntax is the primary crash fix, and the tests do not isolate it. The tests only assert that no diagnostic is raised and that the resolver exists, so they do not show that the guard is what stops the crash. The other fixes (ReportIfLocatedInCompilation, GetPropertyIdentifierLocation, FirstOrDefault) could mask its removal: the unguarded path would reach GetObjectInfo, and the diagnostic paths would no longer throw. The tests would then likely still pass, but wrongly, and the generator might emit a formatter for the external generic type. The tests do not assert that no formatter is generated for the metadata generic type.

receipt_plan.detail: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/TypeCollector.cs:641 remove-guard: if (type.OriginalDefinition.DeclaringSyntaxReferences.IsEmpty) { return; } -> removed; expected to survive because the other null-safe location fixes prevent the crash and the tests only check for no warnings plus the resolver hint name, not the absence of a formatter for the metadata generic.

findings.claim: The BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull change (GetPropertyIdentifierLocation) has no test. The unkeyed-member test only covers MemberNeedsKey, and keyless members with neither int nor string keys are never exercised. Mutating the helper back to [0] indexing would survive, since the early-return guard prevents that path from being reached for metadata types.

receipt_plan.detail: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/TypeCollector.cs:991 delete-statement: GetPropertyIdentifierLocation(item) -> ((PropertyDeclarationSyntax)item.DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0].GetSyntax()).Identifier.GetLocation(); expected to survive because the generic early return stops metadata types before this code, and no test hits the null-key diagnostic.

findings.claim: ReportIfLocatedInCompilation has no negative test. No test checks that a source-located diagnostic is still reported (e.g. MsgPack004 on a same-assembly type), so negating the condition or reporting everything would survive. The tests only assert the absence of diagnostics, and for a metadata type no diagnostic is reachable anyway.

receipt_plan.detail: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/TypeCollector.cs:1451 negate-condition: if (diagnostic.Location.IsInSource && this.compilation.ContainsSyntaxTree(...)) -> if (!(...)); expected to survive in these new tests since the metadata-type scenarios emit no diagnostics, though existing analyzer tests may kill it.

no test in the suite detects linq-first at src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/TypeCollector.cs:1440

hunches.claim: The new reportDiagnostic wrapper drops every diagnostic whose location is not in source, not only diagnostics about metadata symbols. `GetPropertyIdentifierLocation` returns null when the property's syntax is not a `PropertyDeclarationSyntax`, which is the case for a positional record parameter property declared in the compiling assembly. So the BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull error for such a source property is now silently dropped instead of being reported, for example `[property: Key((string)null)]` on a positional record parameter. The same applies to any existing diagnostic created with a null or Location.None location for a same-assembly type. This contradicts 'types declared in the same assembly keep working'.

receipt_plan.detail: Write a VerifyCS test with `[MessagePackObject] public record R([property: Key((string)null)] int X);` (LanguageVersion C# 9+) that expects the BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull diagnostic. On head no diagnostic is reported. Also rerun the full existing analyzer test suite to find any diagnostic that previously used Location.None and is now suppressed.

hunches.claim: `ReportIfLocatedInCompilation` now silently drops every diagnostic whose location is not in a tree of this compilation. Consider a `[MessagePackObject]` class declared in source that inherits from a base class in a referenced assembly, where the base has a public member with no [Key]. The MemberNeedsKey (MsgPack004) diagnostic for the inherited member gets location null (from `FirstOrDefault()`) and is discarded. The user's own source type then gets no error, even though the base type may not be a MessagePackObject in its own assembly, so nothing reports it there either (contrary to the remark). Falling back to the formatted type's identifier location would keep the error. The same filter also drops any diagnostic deliberately created with Location.None.

receipt_plan.detail: Compile a Lib containing `public class Base { public int X { get; set; } }` to an image reference. In App, declare `[MessagePackObject] public class Derived : Base { [Key(0)] public int Y { get; set; } }`. Run the analyzer and assert that some MsgPack004 is reported in App. On head, no diagnostic is reported.

hunches.claim: ReportIfLocatedInCompilation drops every diagnostic whose location is not in source of this compilation, including diagnostics with Location.None. Existing diagnostics created with null/no location (e.g. MsgPack003/004/005 or other type-level diagnostics where GetIdentifierLocation returns null) were previously reported and now are silently dropped, so users no longer see warnings or errors they saw before. This is a behavior change broader than the metadata-symbol crash.

receipt_plan.detail: Run the existing analyzer tests (MsgPack003/004/005/etc.) and add a case where the diagnostic location is Location.None or comes from a partial or generated syntax tree. Assert the diagnostic is still reported on head as on base. A failing test shows the regression.

hunches.claim: The new early return for any generic type whose OriginalDefinition has no declaring syntax skips all further collection, including generic types from referenced assemblies that previously got a closed-generic formatter registered. A referenced-assembly generic struct without its own resolver, or one that is not a [MessagePackObject], previously went through CollectGeneric and now yields no formatter entry in the generated resolver. This changes generated output users snapshot, and could cause runtime formatter-not-found errors. It also applies to BCL generics such as ValueTuple<,> or KeyValuePair<,> if they reach this point.

receipt_plan.detail: Rerun the generator snapshot tests. Add a sample with a member of type ValueTuple<int,string> or KeyValuePair<,> and a closed generic from a referenced assembly. Compare generated resolver output on base and head for missing GetFormatter entries.

hunches.claim: The guard sits after the custom-formatter and enum checks but the diff context does not show whether it also precedes the handling of built-in generic collections (List<T>, Dictionary<,>, Nullable<T>), which are metadata symbols. If it does, those generic members are skipped, and their type arguments are no longer collected, so user types nested inside them lose generated formatters.

receipt_plan.detail: Generate for a [MessagePackObject] with List<MyType> and Nullable<MyStruct> members, on base and head. Diff the output to confirm MyType's formatter is still registered.

hunches.claim: ReportIfLocatedInCompilation drops every diagnostic whose location is not in a syntax tree of the current compilation, including diagnostics with no location (Location.None). The wrapper applies to all reportDiagnostic calls, so any diagnostic that guards users against insecure or unsupported configurations and lacks a source location is now silently suppressed instead of crashing or reporting. Because the wrapper only filters the analyzer path, the generator output does not change. The suppression could hide a security-relevant diagnostic, but none is evident in the diff, so the impact is low.

receipt_plan.detail: Add an analyzer test where a MessagePackObject has a member that triggers a diagnostic with a null or metadata location (for example MemberNeedsKey on a metadata type). Assert the diagnostic set before and after the change. Also grep reportDiagnostic call sites for any security-relevant rule that can carry Location.None.

hunches.claim: The README and MsgPack004 docs state that diagnostics for referenced-assembly types are reported by the defining assembly. This is consistent with [L8]. However, the new early return runs for all generic types without syntax, and this includes non-MessagePackObject generics that previously went through collection (e.g. closed generics of metadata types with custom formatters are handled earlier, but other paths are now skipped). The docs claim of support is not backed by a generated formatter for the member's type; the doc states the type is usable, but the resolver gets no formatter registration for Item<int>.

receipt_plan.detail: Serialize Cmd with Item<int> member using the head-built generated resolver and verify a formatter for Item<int> is resolved at runtime (not FormatterNotRegistered); compare bytes against a dynamic-resolver round-trip.

hunches.claim: The requirement names three unguarded `DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0]` sites (reporter's lines 735, 1009 and 1101). The diff fixes only two of them: the BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull site at new line 991 and the MemberNeedsKey site at new line 1083. The site corresponding to reporter line 735 (base about 711, head about 717) is not touched. The new `ReportIfLocatedInCompilation` wrapper filters only after `Diagnostic.Create` has run, and the location argument is evaluated first, so it cannot stop that indexing from throwing. That site is only shielded while the new CollectGeneric early return keeps metadata generic types away from `GetObjectInfo`. Another path that reaches `GetObjectInfo` with a metadata member (for example a source type inheriting members from a metadata base type) would still throw. This leaves the acceptance criterion 'Diagnostics that need a source location do not crash when the offending symbol has no declaring syntax' only partly met.

receipt_plan.detail: grep head TypeCollector.cs for `DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0]`. The remaining hit near line 717 (reporter's line 735) is still indexed unguarded inside a diagnostic argument that is evaluated before ReportIfLocatedInCompilation runs.

hunches.claim: suppressed by unconfirmed context entry: [L8] area=analyzer, generator: Types that come from a referenced assembly are deliberately not analysed and get no formatter from the compiling assembly. In `TypeCollector.CollectCore`, after the custom-formatter, enum and generic checks, a non-generic type whose symbol is metadata-only exits with a bare `if (type.Locations[0].IsInMetadata) { return; }` (TypeCollector.cs:367-370), so no MsgPack003/004/005 diagnostic and no generated formatter appear for it. The defining assembly owns validating and formatting its own types (rationale inferred: the code has no comment). A missing diagnostic or formatter for such a type is not a defect. (source: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/TypeCollector.cs:367) (would-be finding: The early return for generic types whose OriginalDefinition has no syntax matches the ledger decision that metadata-only types are deliberately not analysed and get no formatter from the compiling assembly. The missing formatter and diagnostics for such types is deliberate, not a defect.)

receipt_plan.detail: [L8] Types from a referenced assembly are deliberately not analysed and get no formatter; a missing diagnostic or formatter for them is not a defect.
